title: Bagging & Random Forests
html:
Averaging many high-variance models cancels much of their variance. Bagging trains each model on a bootstrap sample; a random forest also restricts each split to a random subset of features so the trees are less alike.

Why averaging works

Var(average of B models) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ² / B σ² = variance of one model, ρ = correlation between models

More trees shrink the second term toward 0 but the first stays: highly correlated trees can't cancel each other's errors. Random feature subsets lower ρ — that is the whole idea of a random forest. Bagging mainly reduces variance; it does little for bias, so it suits deep, low-bias trees.

Bootstrap samples and out-of-bag rows

A bootstrap sample draws n rows with replacement. Each row is left out with probability (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e ≈ 0.368, so each tree sees about 63.2% of the distinct rows. The unseen ~36.8% are that tree's out-of-bag (OOB) rows — a free validation set.

One tree vs bagging vs random forest

Key hyperparameters

ParameterMeaningGuidance
n_estimatorsNumber of treesMore never overfits — it only stops improving; a few hundred is typical
max_featuresFeatures considered at each split"sqrt" (classifier default); lower → less correlated trees. Note RandomForestRegressor defaults to 1.0 (all features = plain bagging)
max_depth, min_samples_leafTree sizeDefaults grow full trees; limit them on noisy data
class_weightWeights for imbalanced classes"balanced" or "balanced_subsample"
n_jobsParallel trainingTrees are independent — bagging parallelises perfectly
Watch out

feature_importances_ (mean decrease in impurity) is computed on training data and is biased toward continuous and high-cardinality features. Prefer permutation importance on held-out data (see Explainability).

Do

Use as a strong, low-effort default for tabular data: little tuning, no scaling, robust to outliers, OOB estimate included.

Avoid

Expect it to extrapolate beyond the training range, to be small or fast at prediction time with thousands of deep trees, or to be as interpretable as one tree. ExtraTreesClassifier (random thresholds too) is a faster, even more randomised cousin.

Why does a random forest generalise better than a single decision tree?

Each deep tree has low bias but high variance. Averaging many trees trained on bootstrap samples, with a random subset of features at each split to decorrelate them, cancels much of that variance while keeping the bias low.

What is the out-of-bag score?

Each tree skips ~37% of the rows in its bootstrap sample. Predicting each row using only the trees that didn't see it gives an almost free validation estimate, similar to cross-validation.

Can adding more trees to a random forest overfit?

No — adding trees only reduces the variance of the average; the error converges to a limit. The forest can still overfit through its individual trees (too deep on noisy data), which is controlled with depth/leaf-size settings.
